newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan blames lawmakers for futures market delay.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan blames lawmakers for futures market delay.

text.p: Taiwan's financial market regulator on Monday blamed an apparently deadlocked parliament for yet another delay in establishing Taiwan's first futures exchange, now aiming to open in October.

"We have decided to delay our target date to open Taiwan's futures exchange to October," Securities and Exchange Commission official Lo Chien-an told Reuters on Monday. "The slow legislative process delayed the market establishment."
It was only in October that the watchdog body, in a bout of optimism, advanced the target date to July from late 1997.
Taiwan is under pressure to set up its own futures exchange in a broad financial liberalisation but faces a key obstacle -- the lack of a futures exchange law to govern its operations.
A draft law has passed a Legislative Yuan committee but the full parliament has yet to begin to review a final version with only days left before the year-end recess.

At least three drafts backed by the ruling Nationalist Party or the opposition Democratic Progressive Party are vying for passage, and analysts have declined to predict when -- or even if -- a compromise might emerge.
Racing to fill the gap, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Singapore International Monetary Exchange both plan to launch Taiwan stock index-linked futures contracts in January 1997.

That would give the CME and SIMEX contracts a nine-month head start over any stock index derivatives offered in Taiwan. Even a plan to list stock-index options in the main Taiwan stock exchange is not likely to launch before October.
Analysts estimate Taiwan stock-index futures could generate T$50 billion (US$1.8 billion) a month in first-year turnover.
Lo acknowledged the increasing pressure on Taiwan, but said the matter was up to parliament. "We are racing against time, but we must have the law before we can establish a market."
Plans by the CME and SIMEX have tempted regulators to try to step up regulatory control to protect the slow-developing Taiwan market from such aggressive offshore rivals.

Without calling the CME and SIMEX projects hostile, Taiwan has threatened to cut off access to Taiwan stock market price data used to compile the indices on which their contracts will be based in a move to undermine their market viability.

The CME contracts will use the Dow Jones Taiwan Index compiled by Dow Jones and Co Inc, while the SIMEX will use the Taiwan Index of Morgan Stanley Capital International, a unit of Morgan Stanley Group Inc.

Taiwan still bans trading in unauthorised futures contracts, and officials are fully aware of the difficulty they would face in trying to police investors seeking to trade offshore contracts through overseas brokerages.

Officials have said the commisison would continue to talk with the CME and SIMEX, hoping to reach a mutually advantageous plan for a simultaneous launch of local and offshore Taiwan stock-index derivatives with equal access by all.
The Chicago and Singapore exchanges have stood by their plans to launch on schedule in January.
